title: Checking the sums
objectives: Check an AI answer's arithmetic with an estimate, and recompute it when it matters.

screens.prose: A chatbot is asked how £2,400 grows at 3% a year, compounded, for 5 years. Before you work anything out, estimate.

lines: You: I put £2,400 in an account paying 3% a year, compounded. What will it grow to in 5 years?
Chatbot: After 5 years it will grow to £2,760.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Roughly how much does 3% a year for 5 years add, compounded?

options.text: A little more than 15%, since each 3% is on a bigger sum
Exactly 15%, since 5 times 3% makes 15% in all
options.why: You added the five 3%s. Each year's 3% is on the grown sum, so the total is a little more.

options.text: Just 3%, the yearly rate
options.why: That is one year. Five years add far more.

options.text: A little less than 15%
options.why: Growth on growth adds a little, never takes away, when the rate is positive.

hints.text: Is the second year's 3% taken on £2,400 or on more?
Growth on growth, as in ratio.
Five 3%s make 15%, and the interest on interest adds a little more.

feedback.correct: A little over 15%, so a little over £2,760.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall growth on growth.

explain.text: Five years at 3% is 15% if nothing compounds. Each year's interest also earns interest, so the true rise is a little more than 15%. So the answer should be a little above £2,760, and the chatbot gave exactly £2,760.

screens.prose: Slide the years. One point adds 3% of £2,400 each year (simple interest); the other adds 3% of the growing balance (compound).

derive.caption: After {{n}} years: simple {{money(2400 * (1 + 0.03 * n), "£", 2)}}, compound {{money(2400 * pow(1.03, n), "£", 2)}}

screens.question: Slide to 5 years. Which point lands on the chatbot's £2,760?

options.text: The simple-interest point
The compound point
options.why: At 5 years the compound point is at £2,782.26, past £2,760.

options.text: Both points
options.why: They part company after year 1. Only one is at £2,760.

options.text: Neither point
options.why: Slide to 5 and read the caption: one of them is at £2,760.00.

hints.text: Slide to 5 and read the caption.
Compare both figures with £2,760.
Simple interest gives £2,760.00 at 5 years; compounding gives £2,782.26.

feedback.correct: The chatbot used simple interest, though you asked for compound.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to 5 years and read the caption.

explain.text: Simple interest adds £72 a year: $2400 \times (1 + 5 \times 0.03) = 2760$. Compounding adds 3% of a growing balance and reaches £2,782.26. The chatbot's figure is the simple one.

screens.prose: Two checks catch most slips. **Estimate first**: does the answer land where it should? **Recompute exactly** when the number matters. The estimate said "a little over £2,760"; now recompute.
screens.question: Work out $2400 \times 1.03^5$ to the nearest penny.

hints.text: Multiply by 1.03 five times.
A calculator helps: $1.03^5 \approx 1.159274$.
$2400 \times 1.159274 = 2782.26$ to the nearest penny.

feedback.correct: $2400 \times 1.03^5 = 2782.26$, inside the estimate band. The chatbot was £22.26 short.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply £2,400 by 1.03 five times.

byKey.simple: That is the chatbot's simple-interest figure. Compounding multiplies by 1.03 each year.
byKey.four-years: You multiplied by 1.03 four times. Five years need five.
byKey.interest-only: That is the interest alone. The question asks for the balance.

explain.text: Multiplying by 1.03 five times gives $2400 \times 1.03^5 = 2782.26$. It sits inside the band from £2,760 to £2,784 that the estimate gave. So the estimate caught the slip and the exact figure fixed it.

screens.prose: A chatbot says 17% of £4,850 is £971.50. Build 17% from 10%, 5% and 2%, as in ratio.
screens.question: What is 17% of £4,850?

hints.text: What is 10% of £4,850?
10% is £485, so 5% is half of that.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find 10%, 5% and 2%, then add.

byKey.bot: That is the chatbot's figure. Build 17% yourself from 10%, 5% and 2%.
byKey.twenty: That is 20% of £4,850, close to the chatbot's slip. 17% is less.
byKey.tenth: The decimal point slipped one place. 10% of £4,850 is £485, not £48.50.
byKey.no-two: You added 10% and 5% only. 17% needs the 2% as well.

explain.text: 10% is £485, 5% is £242.50 and 2% is £97, so 17% is £824.50. The chatbot's £971.50 is about 20% of £4,850. A quick build like this catches a wrong figure in under a minute.

screens.prose: A share fell from £80 to £60. A chatbot says it fell 33.3%. Recall from ratio which value a percentage change is measured against.
screens.question: By what percentage did the share fall?

hints.text: Which value did the move start from?
Divide the change by the start.
£20 out of the starting £80 is 25%.

feedback.correct: $20 / 80 = 0.25$, a 25% fall. The chatbot divided by the end value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the change by the starting value.

byKey.new-base: That is the chatbot's 33.3%: £20 over the end value £60. A change is measured against where it started, £80.
byKey.pounds: You turned the £20 fall into 20%. Divide it by the start, £80.

explain.text: A percentage change compares the change with the starting value: $20 / 80 = 0.25$, so 25%. The chatbot divided by the end value: $20 / 60 \approx 0.333$. Ask yourself which base a figure uses.

screens.prose: A chatbot adds a column of five monthly costs and says the total is £4,770. Estimate first: round each cost to the nearest £100.
screens.question: The chatbot dropped one row. Tap it.

hints.text: What do the five costs add to, each rounded to the nearest £100?
The true total is £5,530.

feedback.correct: The true total is £5,530; £5,530 − £4,770 = £760, July's cost.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the column, then find the gap.

byKey.r0: Without April the total would be £4,290, not £4,770.
byKey.r1: Without May the total would be £4,545, not £4,770.
byKey.r2: Without June the total would be £4,115, not £4,770.
byKey.r4: Without August the total would be £4,400, not £4,770.

explain.text: Rounding each cost to the nearest £100 gives 1,200 + 1,000 + 1,400 + 800 + 1,100 = £5,500, so £4,770 looks about £700 short. The exact total is £5,530, and the gap of £760 is July. Estimating first flagged it; recomputing found it.

screens.prose: Back to the £2,760. A colleague types "Are you sure?" and the chatbot replies "Yes, I am sure: £2,760." Another time it replies "Apologies, it is £2,782.26."

lines: You: I put £2,400 in an account paying 3% a year, compounded. What will it grow to in 5 years?
Chatbot: After 5 years it will grow to £2,760.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Is asking "Are you sure?" a check?

options.text: No: either reply is just likely text, so you still recompute
Yes: if it agrees again, the figure is confirmed
options.why: You treated agreement as a check. "Yes, I am sure" is likely text, not a recomputation.

options.text: Yes: if it changes its answer, the new one is right
options.why: A changed answer is also likely text. This time it is right, but you only know that by recomputing.

options.text: Yes, if you ask it twice more
options.why: More replies are more likely text. None of them is a check.

hints.text: How is the reply to "Are you sure?" produced?
Look again at the chatbot's line.
Like any reply, it is likely text. Only an estimate or a recomputation checks a figure.

feedback.correct: Not a check. It may agree or flip; either way you recompute.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how the reply to "Are you sure?" is written.

byKey.yes-agree: You took agreement as a check. The model writes the likely reply to "Are you sure?", which can be "yes" to a wrong figure.

explain.text: A reply to "Are you sure?" is written like any other reply: as likely text. It may stick to a wrong answer or apologise and change a right one. Your own estimate and recomputation are the check.

screens.prose: A chatbot says 15% of £2,400 is £360. You check: 10% is £240 and 5% is £120.
screens.question: Your check agrees with the chatbot. What now?

options.text: Use the figure: the check has confirmed it
Treat the check as wasted time, since it was right
options.why: A check that confirms a figure is a check that worked. You now know it is right.

options.text: Distrust it anyway, since chatbots are often wrong
options.why: You checked it yourself. Distrust after a good check helps no one.

options.text: Ask the chatbot to confirm it as well
options.why: Its confirmation adds nothing to your own check.

hints.text: What is a check for?
Compare the 15% row with the chatbot's row.
Your £240 + £120 = £360 matches. The figure is confirmed, so use it.

feedback.correct: Your check confirms it. Confirming a right figure is the point of checking.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what your check has shown.

explain.text: $240 + 120 = 360$, so the chatbot was right. A check is not only for catching slips: it is what lets you use a figure with confidence.

screens.prose: Keep a tool for checking. Write `compound(principal, rate, years)` that returns the balance after compounding once a year, rounded to 2 places. The rate is a decimal: 3% is `0.03`.
screens.question: Write compound so that the hidden tests pass.

widget.how: Submit runs 5 hidden tests. Each answer is accepted when `math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9)`.

mutants.symptom: Never rounds, so the balance keeps its stray decimals instead of stopping at the penny.

mutants.source:
def compound(principal, rate, years):
    return round(principal * (1 + rate * years), 2)
mutants.symptom: Adds simple interest, the same amount every year, instead of compounding on the growing balance.
Always compounds at least one year, so 0 years returns more than the principal.

hints.text: Start the balance at the principal.
Inside a loop over the years, multiply the balance by (1 + rate).
After the loop, return round(balance, 2). With 0 years the loop never runs.

feedback.correct: Your function compounds once a year and rounds to the penny.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing test: years, rate and rounding are the usual slips.

explain.text: The loop multiplies by $1 + r$ once a year, so it computes $P(1 + r)^n$. With 0 years it returns the principal unchanged. You now have a one-line check for any compound figure a chatbot gives.

screens.prose: The chatbot used simple interest where compound was asked: $$P(1 + nr) \text{ instead of } P(1 + r)^n$$ Two checks catch slips like this: estimate first, then recompute exactly when the number matters.
screens.question: When is it worth recomputing a chatbot's figure exactly?

options.text: When the number will be used for something that matters
Never, if it lands inside your estimate band
options.why: A band only says it is about right. If the exact figure matters, recompute it.

options.text: Only when the chatbot says it is unsure
options.why: It may sound sure and be wrong. Its tone is not the test.

options.text: Only when the number is large
options.why: A small number can matter a lot, such as a rate or a fee.

feedback.correct: Recompute whenever the figure will be used for something that matters.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the figure will be used for.

screens.prose: A junior analyst builds a spreadsheet from a chatbot's figures. One cell says revenue grew 20%, from £40 million to £50 million. Firm and figures are invented.
screens.question: Recompute the growth. What is it, as a percentage?

hints.text: Which year does growth start from?
Divide the £10m change by last year's revenue.

feedback.correct: $10 / 40 = 0.25$: revenue grew 25%. The chatbot divided by this year's £50m.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the change by the starting year.

byKey.new-base: That is the chatbot's 20%: £10m over this year's £50m. Growth is measured from last year, £40m.
byKey.ratio: You divided £50m by £40m, which gives 1.25 times. The growth is the part above 1: 25%.

explain.text: Growth is the change over the starting value: $10 / 40 = 0.25$, so 25%. The chatbot's 20% used the wrong base. A one-minute check before the sheet goes out saves every figure built on it.

ideas: Estimate first: a rough figure tells you where the answer should land, and a slip often lands far away.
Recompute exactly when the number matters. Your own sum, or a small script, is the check.
Asking "Are you sure?" is not a check: the reply is likely text. A check that agrees is a check that worked.
summary.trap: "Are you sure?" is not a check. The model may agree, or flip, either way.

quiz.question: A chatbot says 4% of £6,200 is £2,480. What does a quick estimate say?

options.text: It is far too big: 4% of about £6,000 is about £240
It looks about right for 4% of that amount
options.why: 1% of £6,200 is £62, so 4% is about £250. £2,480 is ten times too big.

options.text: It is too small
options.why: It is too big, by about ten times.

options.text: An estimate cannot tell
options.why: An estimate shows it is ten times too big.

feedback.correct: 4% of £6,200 is £248, so £2,480 is ten times too big: a decimal slip.

explain.text: 1% of £6,200 is £62, so 4% is £248. The chatbot's £2,480 is ten times that: the decimal point moved. An estimate catches it at once.

quiz.question: A chatbot gives a sum. You ask "Are you sure?" and it says yes. Has the sum been checked?

options.text: No: its "yes" is likely text, not a recomputation
Yes: it confirmed the sum
options.why: It wrote the likely reply to your question. Nothing was recomputed.

options.text: Half checked: you should ask once more
options.why: Asking more gives more likely text, not a check.

options.text: Yes, if it answered quickly
options.why: Speed tells you nothing about the sum.

feedback.correct: Not checked. Estimate or recompute it yourself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what "yes" is made of.

explain.text: The reply to "Are you sure?" is written like any reply, as likely text. It may say yes to a wrong sum. Only your own estimate or recomputation checks it.

quiz.question: A chatbot says £1,000 at 10% a year for 2 years, compounded, gives £1,200. What is the right figure?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by 1.1 twice.

byKey.simple: That is simple interest, the chatbot's slip. Compounding adds 10% of £1,100 in year 2.
byKey.interest: That is the interest alone. Add the £1,000.

explain.text: Year 1 adds £100 to make £1,100; year 2 adds 10% of £1,100, which is £110. So the balance is $1000 \times 1.1^2 = 1210$, and the chatbot used simple interest.

quiz.question: Costs fell from £500 to £400. A chatbot says they fell 25%. What is the right figure?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the change by the starting value.

byKey.new-base: That is the chatbot's 25%: £100 over the new £400. Measure from the start, £500.

explain.text: The fall is £100, and a change is measured against where it started: $100 / 500 = 0.2$, so 20%. The chatbot divided by the end value.
